screens.title: Why This Matters
screens.body:
A slide deck read aloud by a screen reader is a completely different experience than one viewed on screen. Someone using assistive technology (AT) hears your slides in whatever order the software decides they belong in - not necessarily the order they're arranged on the canvas - and can't rely on color, position, or a quick glance to understand what's going on.

PowerPoint also has its own accessibility quirks that don't come up in a document or spreadsheet: reading order isn't just top-to-bottom, individual shapes often need to be grouped before AT can read their alt text at all, and a live presentation adds a whole additional layer - captions, audio description, and what the presenter says out loud - on top of the slide file itself.

The good news is the same as with any Office file: this is almost entirely about using PowerPoint's built-in tools (layouts, the Reading Order pane, alt text, real lists and tables) the way they're designed to be used, rather than building slides by hand with plain text boxes and manual spacing.

This module walks through the issues that come up most often, one at a time. Each screen covers one concept: what the problem is, and exactly how to fix it. A short quiz follows once you've been through all of them.

screens.title: Give Every Slide a Real Title
Reading Order
screens.body:
Reading order is one of the areas that most directly affects how usable your slides are for AT - it's the order objects are actually announced in, and it's easy to assume it just follows the visual layout. It doesn't.

**On Windows:** Open the **Reading Order** pane (**Review** tab). It lists every object on the slide in the order it will be read, and lets you drag them into the order you actually want.

**On Mac:** Open **Home > Arrange > Selection Pane**. {{answer:ppt-q2}}A screen reader reads objects in the *reverse* of the order they're listed in the Selection Pane{{/answer}} - the bottom item in the list is read first, not the top. Drag items in the pane to fix the order.

**Do:** First arrange the *visual* layout of the slide the way you want it to read (top to bottom, left to right, or however it's meant to flow), then use the Reading Order or Selection Pane to make the announced order match that.

**Don't:** Assume that objects positioned correctly on screen will automatically be read in that same order - reading order is tracked completely separately from visual position.

screens.title: Alt Text for Images and Objects
screens.body:
Alt text works the same way in PowerPoint as it does anywhere else in Office: a screen reader speaks it in place of a visual you can't see. In a slide deck, that need shows up in more places than just plain pictures.

{{answer:ppt-q3}}Alt text is needed on pictures, clip art, charts and graphs, SmartArt, embedded objects, and video or audio files - essentially anything visual that isn't purely decorative.{{/answer}}

**Do:**

- Select the object, right-click, and choose **View Alt Text** (or **Format Picture > Alt Text** depending on the object type) to open the description field.
- Keep it brief - a short sentence or two describing what the object shows and why it's there.
- On Windows, PowerPoint can auto-generate a starting description for photos and stock images - review and edit it rather than leaving it as-is, and delete any leftover "Description automatically generated" text.

**Don't:**

- {{answer:ppt-q4}}Start a description with "image of" or "picture of"{{/answer}} - a screen reader already announces that it's an image.
- Rely on the **Title** field in the alt text dialog to carry your description - AT doesn't reliably read it; put the actual description in the Description box.

**A Mac-specific gap:** unlike Windows, PowerPoint for Mac doesn't auto-generate any alt text suggestions at all - every description has to be written by hand.

screens.title: Marking Decorative Images
screens.body:
Not every image on a slide carries meaning - a background flourish, a spacer, or a purely visual divider adds nothing a screen reader user needs to hear.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q5}}If an image is present only for decoration or layout, mark it as decorative instead of writing a description for it - this tells screen readers to skip it entirely, exactly as if it weren't there.{{/answer}} The option lives in the same Alt Text pane used for any other image.

**Don't:** Write a description for an image that conveys no real information, or leave its alt text field blank instead of marking it decorative - a blank description can still get announced as "unlabeled image", which is more confusing than skipping it.

screens.title: Long Descriptions for Complex Charts
screens.body:
A simple photo might only need a sentence of alt text. A chart, graph, or infographic packed with data usually needs more explanation than a screen reader user can absorb from a single alt text field.

**Do:**

- Write a short alt text description as you would for any image - just enough to say what the chart shows.
- {{answer:ppt-q6}}Then put the fuller explanation somewhere else the audience can actually reach it: in nearby text on the slide, in the slide's Notes, or on an appendix slide at the end of the deck.{{/answer}} A table showing the same data the chart displays is often the clearest option.
- If the longer explanation lives somewhere else in the deck, say so in the alt text itself ("see the data table in the Appendix") so a listener knows where to go.

**Don't:** Try to cram a full explanation of a complex chart into the alt text field alone - keep alt text short, and put the detail where it has room to breathe.

screens.title: Screenshots
screens.body:
A screenshot is really just another image, so the same alt text and decorative-vs-meaningful rules from earlier apply - but a screenshot has its own extra wrinkle: text baked into a screenshot (a menu label, an error message, a paragraph of on-screen text) can't be read as text by AT at all, no matter how good the surrounding alt text is.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q29}}When a screenshot's alt text needs to convey more than just what it visually shows - the exact wording of an error message, values typed into a form, the steps in a multi-step dialog - write that text out in the description itself, rather than describing the screenshot only in general terms.{{/answer}}
- Crop a screenshot down to just the relevant portion of the window or screen, and enlarge it if needed - a screenshot shrunk to fit a slide often becomes too small to read even for sighted viewers.
- Consider whether the key information would actually be clearer as real, typed text or a real table on the slide instead of an image of it - a screenshot of a settings dialog is sometimes better replaced by simply listing the two or three settings that actually matter.
- If a screenshot shows a lengthy or complex sequence, use the same long-description approach from the previous screen - a short alt text summary, with the full detail in nearby text, the Notes pane, or an appendix slide.
- {{answer:ppt-q30}}When presenting a screenshot live, say out loud whatever you'd otherwise only point at or highlight on screen - name the specific button, field, or line of text directly ("the Save button in the bottom-right", not just "this button here") - and read aloud the same key on-screen text you already transcribed into the alt text.{{/answer}}

**Don't:** Write alt text for a screenshot that only describes its general appearance ("a screenshot of a dialog box") when the actual text inside it is the entire point of including it.

screens.title: Grouping Objects
screens.body:
This one is specific to PowerPoint: alt text applied to an individual shape often isn't read by assistive technology at all. If a piece of your slide is actually built from several separate shapes - an icon made of overlapping circles, a diagram assembled from boxes and arrows - AT may not pick up any of it.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q7}}Select every shape that makes up the visual, group them into a single object (right-click > **Group**, or the **Group** button on the **Shape Format** tab), and add one alt text description to that group{{/answer}} describing the whole thing - including the order and relationship of the pieces inside it, the same way you would for a complex image.

**Don't:** Leave a multi-shape graphic ungrouped and add alt text to its individual pieces, expecting AT to read all of them - group first, then describe the result as one object.

screens.title: Use Images to Support the Message, Not Distract From It
screens.body:
Accessibility isn't only about making an image *readable* by AT - a slide that's visually cluttered, or full of images that don't add anything real, is harder for everyone to follow, sighted or not.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q28}}Only add an image when it genuinely illustrates or reinforces the point you're making - a photo, chart, or diagram a listener could safely skip without losing anything isn't earning its place on the slide.{{/answer}}
- Choose a simple, focused image over a busy one - a photo crowded with unrelated detail is harder to describe in alt text, and harder to take in visually, for the same reason.
- Keep the number of images on one slide small, for the same reason a wall of bullet points is a problem - too many competing visuals raise how much a viewer (or a listener working through several alt text descriptions in a row) has to process at once.
- Make sure an image and the slide's text are clearly making the same point, not two different ones at the same time.

**Don't:** Add generic clip art or stock photography just to fill empty space - a purely decorative image that doesn't relate to the content adds visual noise without adding meaning, and (as covered earlier) should be marked decorative rather than described at all.

screens.title: Master Slide and Background Content
screens.body:
The Slide Master lets you set a consistent look - colors, fonts, a logo, a footer - across every slide in the deck at once. It's a great accessibility tool for keeping things consistent, with one important catch.

{{answer:ppt-q8}}Text and images placed on the Slide Master itself are never read by assistive technology, no matter how meaningful they are - only content on the actual presentation slide gets announced.{{/answer}}

**Do:**

- If something on the master slide actually conveys meaning (a logo, a revision date, anything more than decoration), add an equivalent on the real slide too - either as visible text, or as a small placeholder image with the same alt text.
- You only need to do this once, on the first slide - repetitive footer-style content doesn't need to be repeated on every single slide after that.

**Don't:** Assume that because a logo or label appears on every slide via the master, AT users are hearing it too - they aren't, unless it also exists on the slide itself.

screens.title: Real Lists, Not Typed Bullets
screens.body:
Just like in Word or Excel, {{answer:ppt-q9}}items grouped as a real bulleted or numbered list get announced as a list by AT - a screen reader will say something like "list, 5 items" before reading the entries{{/answer}}, giving a listener real context they don't get from plain typed characters.

**Do:** Use PowerPoint's own **Bullets** or **Numbering** buttons (**Home** tab) to build lists, including sub-lists via the indent/increase-indent controls.

**Don't:**

- Type an asterisk, dash, or number in front of each line by hand - a screen reader just reads that character as text, with no indication a list is present at all.
- Insert a plain, un-bulleted paragraph in the middle of a list - it breaks AT's count of how many items the list actually has.

screens.title: Don't Use Color Alone
screens.body:
Coding a status red for "over budget" and green for "on budget", with no other difference, feels intuitive - but it depends entirely on being able to see and distinguish color. A screen reader never announces color at all, and colorblind audience members may not be able to tell the colors apart either way.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q10}}Always pair a color-coded meaning with a second, non-color indicator - a text label, a symbol, or a pattern - so the information doesn't disappear for anyone who can't perceive the color difference.{{/answer}} "Over Budget" written out, or a distinct icon next to each status, works regardless of how someone perceives color.

**Don't:** Use color as the only way to distinguish two things on a slide, whether that's status, importance, or a correct vs. incorrect answer.

screens.title: Color Contrast
screens.body:
Strong contrast between text and its background matters even more on a slide than in a document - it's often read from across a room, or through a screen-share compression, on top of everything low vision or color blindness already affects.

**Do:**

- Use PowerPoint's built-in **Design Ideas** and themes where you can - they're already checked for accessible contrast, which a fully custom background color behind default text usually isn't.
- {{answer:ppt-q11}}Check contrast in charts and graphs too, not just body text - a low-contrast slice color or gridline can be just as unreadable as low-contrast text.{{/answer}}
- Run **Review > Check Accessibility** (covered later in this module) to flag insufficient contrast automatically.

**Don't:** Assume a color combination is fine just because it looks fine on your own monitor - test it, especially anywhere you've moved away from a built-in theme.

screens.title: Fonts, Size, and Simple Layout
screens.body:
A slide is usually read from farther away, or in a smaller screen-share window, than a document on a desk - text sizing that would be fine on paper can be genuinely unreadable projected across a room.

**Do:**

- Use a plain sans-serif font such as Arial or Calibri.
- {{answer:ppt-q12}}Use at least 20pt for body text - treat that as an absolute floor, not a target, and consider going well beyond it for a live presentation; body text in the 28-32pt range reads comfortably from the back of a room.{{/answer}}
- {{answer:ppt-q24}}Slide titles should be at least double the body text minimum - 40pt or larger - so a title stays clearly distinguishable from body text at a glance and stays readable from a distance.{{/answer}}
- Keep each slide to a handful of short bullets rather than dense paragraphs - one thought per line is easier to both read and listen to.
- Left-align text - justified or centered paragraphs create uneven gaps between words that are harder to track, especially for readers with dyslexia or low vision.
- {{answer:ppt-q27}}Leave the bottom inch and a half or so of the slide free of text and important visuals - live captions are typically overlaid across that band of the screen, and text or an image placed there gets covered up the moment captions turn on.{{/answer}}

**Don't:**

- Use all capital letters, or excessive italics or underlining, for body text.
- Try to fit everything you plan to say onto the slide itself - a slide deck is a visual aid for a presenter, not a transcript of the talk.

screens.title: Avoiding Dense, Text-Heavy Slides
screens.body:
A slide packed with paragraphs of text is hard for anyone to read at a glance - and for someone listening to it read aloud by AT, a dense slide is even harder to follow, since there's no way to skim ahead or reread a phrase that didn't land the first time.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q26}}Use the classic "6x6 rule" as a rough shape to aim for, not a strict pass/fail test: around 6 bullet points of about 6-8 words each. What actually matters is the total amount of text and reading time on the slide, not either number alone - a slide with more, shorter bullets (say, 8 items of 2-5 words) can be perfectly fine, while a slide with only 4 or 5 long, wordy bullets can be just as dense.{{/answer}}
- Break a slide that's grown too dense into two or more slides instead of shrinking the font to fit everything - see the previous screen's own minimum font sizes, which a dense slide is often the reason for wanting to violate.
- Say the supporting detail out loud as the presenter, or put it in the Notes pane, rather than writing it out in full on the slide itself.

**Don't:** Treat a slide as a script to read verbatim, or a document to be printed and read on paper - a slide is a visual aid, not the entire message.

screens.title: Using Tables Correctly
screens.body:
Tables in a slide deck run into the same accessibility issues they do everywhere else in Office - plus, a table often isn't even the best choice on a slide in the first place.

**Do:**

- Consider whether the data could be presented another way first - a short paragraph with a heading is often easier to follow on a slide than a table is.
- If a table is genuinely the right choice, build it with PowerPoint's real **Table** feature (**Insert > Table**), never by pasting a grid of text into a plain text box.
- {{answer:ppt-q13}}Turn on **Header Row** from the **Table Design** tab so column headings are actually marked as headers, not just styled to look bold.{{/answer}}
- Keep the structure simple: one data point per cell, no merged or split cells.

**Don't:** Copy and paste cells directly from an Excel spreadsheet - that usually creates an image or an unstructured block of text instead of a real, readable table.

screens.title: Meaningful Hyperlinks
screens.body:
Just like in a document, screen reader users often scan a list of every link on a slide by itself, hearing only the link text - not the sentence around it.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q14}}Make the link text itself describe where it goes - for example, the full phrase "Read the 2025 Annual Report" as the link, not the words "click here" tacked onto the end of a sentence.{{/answer}}
- If the slide might be printed or the audience can't click through live, consider placing the full URL near the link text (or on an appendix slide) so it can be copied by hand.

**Don't:** Use generic link text like "Click Here" or "Learn More" on its own - with more than one link on a slide, there's no way to tell them apart out of context.

**Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl (PC) or Command (Mac) + K opens the hyperlink dialog.

screens.title: Designate the Correct Language
Animation and Transitions
screens.body:
Animation can add visual interest, or walk an audience through a multi-step idea one piece at a time - but it needs to be set up carefully to stay usable, and some of it can be genuinely dangerous.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q16}}Set each animation to start **On Click** (Animations tab > Timing pane), not on an automatic delay or a custom trigger{{/answer}} - this lets someone advance at their own pace with either the mouse or the keyboard.
- If a single animated build is hard to make accessible, consider breaking it into several slides instead - one step per slide, each advancing on click.
- Keep transition effects short enough to settle within about five seconds, so AT isn't left trying to read text that's still moving.

**Don't:**

- {{answer:ppt-q17}}Include flashing or blinking content faster than three flashes per second - faster than that can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.{{/answer}}
- Rely on PowerPoint's built-in checkbox or form-style controls for interactivity - they're often not reachable by keyboard, and may not be read correctly by screen readers at all.

screens.title: Video, Audio, and Captions
screens.body:
A video embedded in a slide brings its own accessibility needs on top of everything else in this module.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q18}}Add captions or subtitles to the video file itself *before* inserting it into PowerPoint{{/answer}} - PowerPoint can't attach a separate caption file to a video the way some other tools can.
- Provide an audio description track (or narrate the important visual details yourself) for any meaning the video conveys only visually, for viewers who are blind or have low vision.
- Interpret meaningful audio in voice or ASL, matching whichever is the primary language of your audience.

**Don't:** Run **Compress Media** or **Optimize Media Compatibility** on a video and assume its captions survived - both features are known to strip out captions and alternate audio tracks, so re-check the video afterward if you use either one.

screens.title: Embedded and Copied-In Objects
screens.body:
It's common to pull content from another file type - a spreadsheet, a PDF, a document - straight into a slide. Done the wrong way, this can quietly break both keyboard access and how correctly AT reads the result.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q19}}Use PowerPoint's actual object types for pasted-in content - for example, a real Table object for spreadsheet data - rather than copying it in as a flat image or an unstructured block.{{/answer}}
- If a file truly needs to be embedded (double-clickable to open in its own program), also make that same file available separately, with instructions for how to get it - an embedded object may not be reachable by keyboard or read correctly by AT at all.

**Don't:** Copy content from another file type into a slide without checking what it actually became - a quick visual match to the source file isn't the same as a real, accessible object underneath it.

screens.title: Use the Built-In Accessibility Checker
Accessible Alternative Formats
screens.body:
Once your deck itself is in good shape, offering it in more than one format gives your audience the option that works best for however they're accessing it.

**Do:**

- When exporting to PDF, use the export option that enables accessibility tagging (for example, checking "Enable accessibility and reflow" in an Acrobat export, or your PDF tool's equivalent) rather than a plain print-to-PDF - {{answer:ppt-q21}}a plain print-to-PDF strips out headings, alt text, and structure the same way it does from Word{{/answer}}.
- If a tagged PDF export isn't available to you, PowerPoint's **Outline View** can be copied into a Word or plain-text document as a fallback - number each slide and paste in its alt text alongside it.
- {{answer:ppt-q31}}Share the deck itself, or an accessible alternate format of it, with attendees ahead of the live session, not only afterward - it lets anyone who needs to review it at their own pace, and with their own assistive technology, instead of only experiencing it in real time during the presentation.{{/answer}}

**Don't:** Treat a plain, untagged PDF export as an accessible substitute for the deck - check that headings and image descriptions actually carried over before sharing it.

screens.title: Presenting Accessibly
screens.body:
An accessible slide file is only half the picture - how you actually present it matters just as much, especially for anyone following along by listening rather than looking.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q22}}Describe what's visually on the slide out loud as you present it, including reading the important alt text you wrote{{/answer}} - if someone lost their video feed entirely and could only hear you, what would they need to know?
- Say "next slide" (or similar) out loud each time you advance, so a listener always knows a change just happened.
- Pace yourself and pause where needed for captioners or interpreters to keep up.

**Don't:** Assume the slide alone carries the meaning - treat your spoken description as part of the talk, not an afterthought bolted on for accessibility's sake.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.body:
A condensed summary of everything in this module - useful to keep open while you're actually building a deck.

- **Titles:** Every slide needs a real Title placeholder, uniquely worded - never fake one with a plain text box.
- **Reading order:** Set it explicitly with the Reading Order pane (Windows) or Selection Pane (Mac, reversed order) - it never automatically matches the visual layout.
- **Alt text:** Right-click > View Alt Text on pictures, charts, SmartArt, embedded objects, and video. Mark purely decorative images as decorative. Put long descriptions of complex charts in nearby text, Notes, or an appendix slide.
- **Grouping:** Multi-shape graphics need to be grouped into one object before alt text on them will be read at all.
- **Master slide:** Anything meaningful placed there also needs a real equivalent on the actual slide - AT never reads the master slide itself.
- **Lists:** Use the Bullets/Numbering buttons, never typed *, -, or 1. by hand.
- **Color:** Never rely on color alone - always add a text label, symbol, or pattern. Check contrast in both text and charts.
- **Fonts and layout:** Sans-serif, 18pt minimum (more for live presentations), left-aligned, one thought per line.
- **Tables:** Real Table objects only, with Header Row turned on - never pasted-in Excel cells.
- **Hyperlinks:** Descriptive text that names the destination, not "Click Here".
- **Language:** Set the correct proofing language, especially for multilingual decks.
- **Animation:** On Click timing only, never automatic or trigger-based. No flashing faster than 3 times a second.
- **Video:** Captions baked into the file before inserting - re-check them after Compress Media.
- **Embedded objects:** Use real PowerPoint object types, and offer a truly embedded file separately too.
- **Before sharing:** Run the Accessibility Checker (Review tab) and export to a tagged, accessible PDF - not a plain print-to-PDF.
- **While presenting:** Describe visuals out loud, announce slide changes, and pace yourself for interpreters and captioners.

When you're ready, start the quiz to check your understanding.
